correctness.rationale: The source loss accumulator and SPD eigenmode update are exact. Initial b greater than learning rate times largest curvature makes every modal multiplier positive and contracting. The general O(sqrt(t)) upper bound on b forces summability of the objective gaps. Exact target then gives a finite accumulator and geometric modal products; fixed target error yields squared-accumulator linear drift plus a convergent correction. Taylor expansion of the modal log-product gives the square-root exponential and the second-order logarithmic power, with finite nonzero multiplicative limit. A standalone checker reconstructs these statements and numerical limiting constants.

originality.rationale: The defining AdaLoss analysis proves geometric convergence with a correctly centered squared-residual accumulator; it motivates the target as a surrogate optimum but does not treat persistent target error. The closest gradient-norm accumulator and stochastic Polyak step papers use different recurrences. The new claim is a mode-by-mode exact dichotomy between geometric and stretched-exponential rates, with the logarithmic prefactor and sharp objective-gap asymptotic. Focused public and indexed searches did not reveal an implication-equivalent claim; unindexed derivations remain a residual risk.
residual_risks: An unindexed optimizer note may have derived the same basic rate classification for loss-target accumulation.
The theorem describes a deterministic quadratic, not changing stochastic losses.
The phase transition is proved in the stated stable-multiplier regime; outside-basin overestimation is not classified.

value.rationale: AdaLoss explicitly replaces gradient-norm feedback by a loss gap relative to a supplied surrogate optimum. The accuracy of that surrogate is mathematically motivated: shifting only objective values leaves the optimization problem and all gradients unchanged, yet the result proves it changes the entire convergence class. The theorem provides exact mode-dependent rates, including a universal square-root exponent and log prefactor, for both under- and overestimation inside natural domains. This is a useful sensitivity benchmark for loss-based adaptive steps, not a mere normalization or first-step check.
